title: The RESP rules that can be worth thousands
summary: Highlights: An RESP covers a lot more than a university degree. Trade schools, occupational programs and some schools abroad all count. A rule tied to your child’s fifteenth birthday can shut off two years of CESG eligibility. Two provinces add their own money on top, and one federal benefit needs no contributions at all.
body_markdown:
#### **Highlights:**


- An RESP covers a lot more than a university degree. Trade schools, occupational programs and some schools abroad all count.
- A rule tied to your child’s fifteenth birthday can shut off two years of CESG eligibility.
- Two provinces add their own money on top, and one federal benefit needs no contributions at all.


You opened an RESP. You set up the transfer. Most months you don’t think about it, and when you do, it’s a line on a statement between the TFSA and the RRSP.


Meanwhile there are rules attached to it that decide whether a few thousand dollars of government money lands in there or doesn’t. Some of them have deadlines. Here’s what you need to know.


## **The RESP is not just a university fund**


Most parents picture a lecture hall.


For full-time study,[CRA’s test](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/individuals/topics/registered-education-savings-plans-resps/payments-resp.html) is three consecutive weeks and 10 hours a week. Part-time has its own rule. Some schools abroad have longer minimums.


Universities and colleges count. So do institutions certified by Employment and Social Development Canada that teach occupational skills without granting credits. Distance education counts. Qualifying schools abroad count.


And it doesn’t only pay tuition. Rent, books, tools and transportation are all eligible.


Trade school counts. So does the program they switch to after dropping the first one.


## **The grant, and the birthday that ends it**


The[Canada Education Savings Grant](https://www.canada.ca/en/services/benefits/education/education-savings/estimating-amounts.html) adds 20% to what you put in, up to $500 a year, capped at $7,200 per child. Lower-income families can get up to another $100 a year.


Unused basic grant room piles up. If there’s enough unused room, up to $5,000 of contributions in a year can attract up to $1,000 of basic CESG.


Then there’s the rule most people find out about too late.


To get the grant in the years your child is 16 and 17, one of two things has to already be true before the end of the year they turn 15. Either at least $2,000 was contributed and left in the RESP, or at least $100 was contributed and left in during each of any four earlier years.


Miss both and you can’t receive CESG on contributions made when they’re 16 or 17.


If your kid is coming up on 15 and the account is thin, check those numbers before December 31 of the year they turn 15.


## **Check what your province adds**


**Quebec** pays the[Québec Education Savings Incentive](https://www.revenuquebec.ca/en/citizens/tax-credits/quebec-education-savings-incentive/) , a refundable tax credit paid straight into the RESP, up to $3,600 per child over their lifetime. Your provider has to offer it. Worth confirming yours does.


**British Columbia** pays a one-time $1,200. You apply between your child’s sixth birthday and the day before their ninth, and you both have to be B.C. residents when you apply. Narrow window, and it closes.


Those two are the only provincial benefits the federal government currently lists.


Then there’s the **Canada Learning Bond** , which works differently from all of it. Income-tested, up to $2,000, and you don’t have to contribute a cent to get it. If a family qualified and nobody applied, that money may still be sitting there unclaimed. It’s retroactive, and once they turn 18, eligible kids can claim it themselves right up to the day before they turn 21.


That changes in 2028. From April, the government will[open an RESP automatically](https://www.canada.ca/en/services/benefits/education/education-savings/canada-learning-bond.html) and deposit the bond for eligible children born in 2024 or later who aren’t already named in a plan by age four. Families of eligible kids born before 2024 will be able to ask for the same thing, though details are still coming. Until then, somebody has to apply.


You apply for all of these through your RESP provider. If you’re not sure the money has actually been landing, ask them.


## **What this buys your kid**


Average tuition for full-time Canadian undergraduate students was $7,734 for 2025/2026, according to[Statistics Canada](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/daily-quotidien/250910/dq250910d-eng.htm) . That’s preliminary, degree programs only, and doesn’t include rent or food.


Whether they pick the program or the cheapest program. Whether they move for school or stay home. Whether they can start something, realize it’s wrong, and switch without it wrecking anything.


That’s what the account is for. It shows up in how much room they have to get something wrong and recover from it.


## **What happens if they don’t go**


Your contributions come back to you tax free. They aren’t income, because that money was already yours. One catch: pull contributions out before your kid is eligible for an educational assistance payment and some CESG may have to go back.


The growth and the grants get taxed in your kid’s hands instead. When they withdraw for school it comes out as an educational assistance payment, and they report it as income. Many students have little or no other income, so the tax bill on EAPs can be small or even zero.


And if school never happens, the growth may still have somewhere to go. Meet the conditions and have enough RRSP room, and you may be able to move up to $50,000 of accumulated income into your RRSP. There’s an RDSP route too, in specific circumstances.


Which ones are open to you depends on your situation, and so does the tax treatment. But you aren’t stuck with one outcome.


## **The catches**


Contributions aren’t deductible. This isn’t an RRSP.


The lifetime limit is $50,000 per child, across every RESP anyone has opened for them, including one a grandparent started that you might not know about. Go over and each subscriber can face a 1% per month tax on their share of the excess until it’s withdrawn.


If your kid never goes, unused CESG generally goes back to the government. Some plans let you share it with a sibling who still has CESG room.


Educational assistance payments are capped at $8,000 total across the first thirteen consecutive weeks of full-time study. Part-time has its own $4,000 limit per thirteen-week period. Those caps cover the government benefits and investment earnings, not every dollar in the account.


## **The grant doesn't invest itself**


When the CESG arrives, it lands as cash in the RESP. It doesn't buy anything. Neither do your own contributions, or the provincial money if you get it. It all sits there until somebody places a trade.


And the grant doesn't show up alongside your contribution. You put money in, the government's 20% follows separately, later, on its own schedule. So even if you're good about buying after your own deposits, the grant can slip past you entirely.


This is the account with the longest runway you own. Cash sitting idle for six months in a TFSA you'll spend next year barely matters. In an RESP for a four-year-old, that's six months of growth you don't get back, repeated every year nobody notices the deposit.
